Q: Don't use asdf if there is no .tool-versions file? A:

Adapted for zsh

# ensure add-zsh-hook is available
autoload -Uz add-zsh-hook

conditional_asdf() {
  if [[ -f .tool-versions ]]; then
    # remove any existing asdf entries then prepend them
    path=(${path:#$HOME/.asdf/shims})
    path=(${path:#$HOME/.asdf/bin})
    path=($HOME/.asdf/shims $HOME/.asdf/bin $path)
  else
    # remove asdf entries when not in a project with .tool-versions
    path=(${path:#$HOME/.asdf/shims})
    path=(${path:#$HOME/.asdf/bin})
  fi
}

# run on directory change and before prompt (covers cd and other cases)
add-zsh-hook chpwd conditional_asdf
add-zsh-hook precmd conditional_asdf

# run once now for this shell
conditional_asdf

Q: `std::span` and static storage for braced initializers (P2752R3) A:

Author of P2752 (and coauthor of P2447) here. Upon reflection I believe Barry's answer is correct. Let me see if I can say it a different way.

At first glance, I thought your example merely fell into the same category as e.g. (Godbolt)

constexpr std::string x = "constexpr in libc++";

Depending on the implementation's choices, this may be constexpr-friendly or not. (See "Just how constexpr is C++20's std::string?" et seq.) Your example is similar, in that P2752 permits but does not require initializer_list<int>{0,0} to be backed by static storage. Today, GCC does the P2752 optimization (thank you GCC devs!) but Clang does not. (Proof 1, proof 2.) However, that's not the whole story: your code is still rejected even by GCC. Yes, GCC is correct to reject it.

You have:

constexpr std::span<const int> sp = {1,2,3};

This is asking the compiler to create a span over the backing array of the initializer_list<int> created from {1,2,3}. This isn't allowed, for basically the same reason that the following isn't allowed:

constexpr std::string_view sv = std::string("foo");

In both cases, you're trying to take a view over the innards of an object that's going to die in a moment, and in both cases, the innards (even if they're physically stored in .rodata) do not, logically, live beyond the lifetime of their owning object. ("Storage is not lifetime.")

In both cases, you can "promote" the object to a global variable with global lifetime and then it's legal to take a view over it (Godbolt):

constexpr std::initializer_list<int> il = {1,2,3};
constexpr std::span<const int> sp = il;  // OK, if unidiomatic

constexpr std::string s = std::string("foo");
constexpr std::string_view sv = s;  // OK

You just can't take a view over the innards of a temporary object. initializer_list does not behave any differently from string in this respect. And because you're trying to do this all at constexpr time, inside the compiler's constexpr interpreter, the compiler is perfectly able to detect these shenanigans and shut you down.

P.S. — in the last Godbolt above we see

constexpr std::initializer_list<int> il1 = {1,2,3};
constinit std::span<const int> sp1 = il1;  // OK, if unidiomatic
constexpr std::initializer_list<int> il2 = {1,2,3};
constinit std::span<const int> sp2 = il2;  // OK, if unidiomatic

constexpr std::string s1 = std::string("foo");
constinit std::string_view sv1 = s1;  // OK
constexpr std::string s2 = std::string("foo");
constinit std::string_view sv2 = s2;  // OK

Notice that on both compilers s1 and s2 naturally have to be their own objects with disjoint storage; whereas GCC makes il1 and il2 share the same backing array, because of P2752 (and Clang doesn't, because Clang doesn't implement P2752 yet).
